---
title: "Week 13 — ML/NLP Visualization"
---

> What a model does beyond its accuracy: how it fails, what it uses, and how sure it is. The week ends by connecting a Streamlit client to the model server from Week 12.

## 📖 Background & Motivation

A trained model reports one number, its accuracy. That number does not say which cases the model gets wrong, what those errors cost, which inputs drive its predictions, or whether its confidence can be trusted. Each of those questions has a standard chart, and this week works through them on two models: a random forest that classifies breast tumors from 30 measurements, and a text classifier that labels movie reviews as positive or negative.

The tumor model shows why the confusion matrix matters more than accuracy: it makes 6 errors on 143 tumors, and 4 of them are cancers it called benign. The review model shows what the same charts look like for text, and why reading a model's confident errors tells you things no metric does. It also shows what a model built on word counts cannot see, such as the word "not", and how a pretrained transformer compares on the same reviews. A short section on clustering covers the case where there are no labels to predict.

The week closes the arc of Weeks 11 and 12. The Streamlit client calls the FastAPI server, and the question becomes what the app should show a user when the model is unsure. That client, server and display together are the architecture of the final project.

---

## 🔎 Learning Objectives

- Read a confusion matrix, and report recall and precision when the two kinds of error cost different amounts.
- Use the ROC curve and a threshold table to show a classification threshold as a choice.
- Compare impurity-based and permutation feature importance, and say which one a chart shows.
- Locate a model's errors with a projection and with a histogram of its predicted probabilities.
- Ask the same questions of a text classifier, including by reading its confident errors.
- Explain one text prediction word by word, and say what a word-count model cannot see that a pretrained transformer can.
- Cluster unlabeled data with K-means and DBSCAN, and report the parameters with the result.
- Connect a Streamlit client to a model server and display the prediction with its uncertainty.

## 💻 Notebook / App Snippets

All of these come from the Block 2 notebook, which runs them in order.

### The confusion matrix, and what a threshold does

```python
from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay

ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_estimator(
    model, X_test, y_test, display_labels=["malignant", "benign"], cmap="Blues")

# Treat malignant as the class we are trying to catch
is_malignant = (y_test == 0)
p_malignant = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 0]

for t in [0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2]:
    called = p_malignant >= t
    print(t, "missed cancers:", int((is_malignant & ~called).sum()),
             "false alarms:", int((~is_malignant & called).sum()))
```

At 0.5 the model misses 4 cancers and raises 2 false alarms. At 0.2 it misses none and raises 9.

### Feature importance, two ways

```python
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

perm = permutation_importance(model, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=30, random_state=0)
compare = pd.DataFrame({"impurity importance": model.feature_importances_,
                        "permutation importance": perm.importances_mean},
                       index=X.columns).sort_values("impurity importance").tail(8)
compare.plot.barh(color=["steelblue", "orange"])
```

The forest ranks area, perimeter and radius highest. Shuffling any one of them barely changes the accuracy, because the three are correlated at 0.98 to 0.99 and the other two still carry the information.

### Reading a text model's confident errors

```python
p_positive = text_model.predict_proba(test_df["text"])[:, 1]
results = test_df.assign(p_positive=p_positive,
                         predicted=(p_positive >= 0.5).astype(int))
results["wrong"] = results["predicted"] != results["label"]
results["sureness"] = (results["p_positive"] - 0.5).abs()

for _, row in results[results["wrong"]].sort_values("sureness", ascending=False).head(3).iterrows():
    print(row["label"], round(row["p_positive"], 2), row["text"][:300], "\n")
```

### Explaining one text prediction

```python
vectorizer = text_model.named_steps["tfidfvectorizer"]
classifier = text_model.named_steps["logisticregression"]

review = test_df["text"][743]
row = vectorizer.transform([review]).toarray()[0]          # one row, 5,000 numbers
contribution = pd.Series(row * classifier.coef_[0],
                         index=vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())[row > 0]

contribution.sort_values().plot.barh()
```

What a word adds to the score is its TF-IDF value in the review times its coefficient. The model calls this positive review positive at 0.95, and the largest push comes from "great", which the writer used in "not great acting" and "not really a great film".

### What word counts cannot see, and a pretrained model

```python
pairs = ["This movie is good.", "This movie is not good."]

text_model.predict_proba(pairs)[:, 1]       # 0.81 and 0.81

from transformers import pipeline
reader = pipeline("sentiment-analysis",
                  model="distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english")
reader(pairs)                               # POSITIVE, then NEGATIVE
```

The word-count model gives both sentences the same score, because `stop_words="english"` removes "not" before the model sees it. DistilBERT reads the words in order and gets both right. On the same 1,000 reviews it scores 0.879 against 0.859. It answers above 0.95 or below 0.05 for 90% of the reviews, and 78 of its 121 errors are among those, so its confidence is less useful than the simpler model's.

### DBSCAN on locations

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

EARTH_RADIUS_KM = 6371.0088
eps_km = 25      # the neighborhood radius; report it with the map

sites["cluster"] = DBSCAN(eps=eps_km / EARTH_RADIUS_KM, min_samples=5,
                          algorithm="ball_tree", metric="haversine"
                          ).fit_predict(np.radians(sites[["lat", "lon"]]))
```

Latitude and longitude are angles, so the distance is measured on the sphere. A label of `-1` means DBSCAN called the site noise.

### Live prediction: Streamlit client → model server

```python
import pandas as pd, requests, streamlit as st

API_URL = st.sidebar.text_input("Server URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8000")
payload = {"sepal_length": 6.0, "sepal_width": 2.7,
           "petal_length": 5.0, "petal_width": 1.7}

if st.button("Predict"):
    try:
        r = requests.post(f"{API_URL}/predict", json=payload, timeout=5)
        r.raise_for_status()
        out = r.json()
        st.success(f"Prediction: {out['prediction']}")
        st.bar_chart(pd.Series(out["probabilities"]))     # the full distribution
    except requests.RequestException as e:
        st.error(f"Could not reach the server: {e}")
```

The field names are the ones the Week 12 server expects. The complete app, with sliders, is `app_live_predictions.py`.

### A client for the detection server

`app_detect_client.py` is the client for Week 12's `detect_server.py`. It sends
an image, gets back every box the model scored, and draws only the ones above a
threshold you set, with a before/after slider between the original and the
annotated image.

```bash
uvicorn detect_server:app --reload        # in the week12 folder
streamlit run app_detect_client.py        # in the week13 folder
```

Start with the sample photo and drag the threshold down from 0.50 to 0.30.
Three more boxes appear, and all three are wrong. The threshold is a decision
the client makes about how much doubt to show, and it re-filters boxes the app
already has: moving it never calls the model again.
